nameStory: This evening primrose earned its 'large-flowered' name from its impressively big yellow blooms that can span up to 4 inches across - much larger than its common cousins. Like other evening primroses, it gets its name from opening its flowers in the evening hours, creating a magical twilight display. The alternate name 'redsepal evening primrose' comes from the reddish tinge often found on the flower sepals (the protective parts beneath the petals).
description: Large-flowered evening primrose is a tall biennial plant that can reach 3-6 feet in height with sturdy, upright stems. It produces spectacular bright yellow flowers that open in the evening and can measure 3-4 inches across - truly impressive blooms that seem to glow in the twilight. The plant forms a rosette of leaves in its first year, then sends up flowering stalks in its second year. Originally from Europe, it has naturalized in scattered locations across New England and is sometimes grown as an ornamental garden plant.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers that are notably large (3-4 inches across) with four heart-shaped petals that feel delicate and papery to the touch. The flowers open in early evening with a sweet, lemony fragrance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lance-shaped leaves arranged alternately on the stem, with a slightly fuzzy texture and prominent white midvein. Lower leaves can be 6-8 inches long with wavy or slightly toothed edges.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, sturdy plant reaching 3-6 feet with thick, reddish-tinged stems that feel substantial and slightly hairy when touched. Forms a ground-hugging rosette in the first year.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Long, cylindrical seed capsules that split open to release numerous small, angular seeds. The capsules make a subtle rattling sound when dry and shaken.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Flower buds are large and elongated with reddish sepals that often have a striped appearance. Buds nod downward before opening upright in the evening.

habitat: Look for large-flowered evening primrose in disturbed soils, roadsides, vacant lots, and garden edges where it has escaped cultivation. It thrives in sandy or well-drained soils and full sun locations. In New England, it's most commonly found near populated areas as an escape from ornamental plantings.

seasonality.spring: First-year plants form low rosettes of fuzzy leaves that emerge in late spring, while second-year plants send up their tall flowering stalks with developing buds.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with the spectacular large yellow flowers opening each evening from June through August, filling the air with sweet fragrance at dusk.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue into early fall, followed by the development and splitting of long seed capsules. Second-year plants die back after setting seed.
seasonality.winter: First-year rosettes may persist under snow cover, while dead stalks from second-year plants remain standing with dried seed capsules that rattle in winter winds.

funFact: The flowers of large-flowered evening primrose open so quickly in the evening that you can actually watch it happen in real-time - the petals unfurl in just a few minutes as the sun sets, like nature's own time-lapse photography show!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with common evening primrose, but large-flowered evening primrose lives up to its name with flowers nearly twice the size. Memory trick: if the yellow flowers are impressively large (bigger than a silver dollar), you've found the large-flowered species.
contextualKnowledge: This plant was historically known as Oenothera lamarckiana and was famous in botanical circles as one of the plants used by Hugo de Vries in his early genetics research. However, scientists now consider that name to be the same species as Oenothera glazioviana.
compareHints: Large-flowered evening primrose stands out from other Oenothera species primarily due to its impressive flower size - much larger than common evening primrose or the various sundrops species. While common evening primrose has 1-2 inch flowers, this species boasts blooms up to 4 inches across. It's also typically taller and more robust than most of its relatives, with thicker stems and larger overall stature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common evening-primrose is the tallest and most robust of New England's evening-primroses, with the largest flowers.
Small sundrops differs from its evening primrose relatives by staying low and sprawling rather than growing tall and upright like common evening primrose.
Among New England's evening primroses, northern evening primrose stands out for its smaller flower size compared to common evening primrose and Large-flowered evening-primrose.
Meadow evening primrose is much less common than its cousin common evening primrose, which grows much taller (3-6 feet) and has larger flowers that open in the evening.
Unlike the bold, large yellow flowers of common evening-primrose that can be 2 inches across, clockweed has tiny, delicate white or pink flowers only half an inch wide.
Unlike its yellow-flowered cousin common evening-primrose which grows tall and upright, pinkladies stays low and spreads horizontally.
Unlike its evening primrose cousins that typically have four-petaled yellow flowers opening at dusk, biennial beeblossom stands out with its pink flowers and incredibly tall, airy growth habit.
Unlike the tall, upright common evening primrose with its simple oval leaves, cutleaf evening primrose stays low to the ground with deeply divided, almost fern-like foliage.
Among the many evening primroses in New England, red-stalked evening primrose stands out primarily for its reddish stem coloration, while most relatives like common evening primrose have green stems.
Unlike the common evening primrose which typically grows 3-5 feet tall, tall evening primrose can reach 6 feet, making it the giant of the genus.
Bigfruit evening primrose stands out dramatically from its New England relatives like common evening primrose due to its sprawling, ground-hugging growth habit rather than upright stems.
Yellow sundrops differ from common evening-primrose by blooming during the day rather than evening and having distinctive blue-green waxy leaves instead of plain green ones.
Among the evening-primroses in New England, Nodding Evening-Primrose is unique for its drooping flower buds - all other species have upright, erect buds.
